Scalable Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training with Automatic Learning Rate Exploration for Large Models

Hailing Cheng Affiliation: LinkedIn Inc. Affiliation: Mountain View, CA 94043 Email: haicheng@linkedin.com    Tao Huang Affiliation: LinkedIn Inc. Affiliation: Mountain View, CA 94043 Email: taohuang@linkedin.com    Chen Zhu Affiliation: LinkedIn Inc. Affiliation: Mountain View, CA 94043 Email: chzhu@linkedin.com    Antonio Alonso Affiliation: LinkedIn Inc. Affiliation: Mountain View, CA 94043 Email: aalonso@linkedin.com
Abstract

Training large neural networks with data-parallel stochastic gradient descent allocates NN GPU replicas to compute effectively identical updates—a practice that leaves the rich space of learning rate configurations entirely unexplored during training. We propose Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training (HDET), a method that repurposes these replicas for simultaneous learning rate exploration at negligible communication overhead. HDET operates in alternating phases: a fan-out stage in which replicas train independently under a structured, symmetric spread of learning rates, and a converge stage in which parameters are averaged across all replicas via AllReduce every TT steps. Building on this ensemble substrate, we further propose an automatic learning rate (auto-LR) controller that treats the relative training loss across replicas as a performance signal, updating the shared base schedule toward higher-performing configurations via a momentum-based gradient-free meta-update. The combined method produces a self-adapting learning rate schedule that improves both optimization quality and generalization without additional hyperparameter sweeps or training budget.

Crucially, the framework generalizes beyond learning rate: any scalar hyperparameter that does not alter model architecture—such as dropout rate, attention scale temperature, or weight-decay coefficient—can be explored across replicas using the same fan-out/converge protocol, with inter-replica loss differences serving as zero-order hypergradients that guide the search direction. HDET is implemented as a drop-in replacement for PyTorch’s OneCycleLR scheduler, requiring no changes to model architecture, optimizer, or data pipeline. Code is available at https://github.com/hailingc/ensemble_training.

1 Introduction

The learning rate schedule is among the most consequential hyperparameter choices in large-model training. Popular schedules—one-cycle annealing (Smith and Topin, 2019), cosine decay (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017), and linear warmup-decay (Vaswani et al., 2017)—must be specified before training begins, leaving practitioners to rely on expensive grid searches or heuristics calibrated on smaller proxy models. Even when a good schedule is found, it may not remain optimal as model or dataset scale changes across training runs.

Simultaneously, large-model training routinely parallelizes across hundreds of GPU replicas using data-parallel stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). In the standard paradigm, every replica maintains an identical copy of the model parameters and advances under an identical learning rate; the replica’s sole distinguishing role is the mini-batch it processes. Beyond improving gradient estimates through a larger effective batch, the additional hardware contributes no qualitative diversity to the optimization trajectory.

We observe that this uniformity is a missed opportunity. The NN parallel replicas could explore NN distinct learning rate trajectories simultaneously, at no additional hardware cost. Moreover, if those diverging trajectories periodically merge through parameter averaging, the resulting model can harvest ensemble-like generalization benefits within a single training run.

We formalize this intuition in Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training (HDET), which interleaves two phases atop any existing DDP+OneCycleLR setup:

  1. 1.

    Fan-out: each of NN GPU replicas trains under a distinct learning rate drawn from a symmetric spread [η¯​(1−α),η¯​(1+α)][\bar{\eta}\,(1-\alpha),\;\bar{\eta}\,(1+\alpha)] around the current base schedule η¯(t)\bar{\eta}^{(t)}, where α≥0\alpha\geq 0 is the spread ratio;

  2. 2.

    Converge: every TT training steps, parameters are averaged across all replicas via AllReduce, producing a unified model that seeds the next fan-out round.

On top of this ensemble substrate we introduce an auto-LR controller that uses the relative training loss across replicas as a performance signal. Replicas with below-average loss receive proportionally higher weight in a softmax-weighted average of per-rank learning rates; the resulting performance deviation drives a momentum-based velocity that shifts the base schedule up or down at each sync point. If high-LR replicas consistently outperform low-LR ones, the base schedule adapts upward; if the opposite holds, it adapts downward. This constitutes a gradient-free, within-run optimizer over the learning rate schedule, eliminating the need for a priori schedule selection.

Contributions.

  • •

    We propose HDET, a training method that transforms existing DDP replicas into a structured learning rate exploration ensemble at zero hardware overhead (§3).

  • •

    We introduce an automatic LR controller that uses rank-wise loss signals to adaptively update the learning rate via a gradient-free momentum update, requiring no additional tuning (§3.4).

  • •

    We identify a practical two-stage strategy—warm noisy initialization from a pre-trained checkpoint followed by HDET ensemble training—that jointly maximizes model quality and training stability: warm initialization seeds each replica near a high-quality solution, while periodic weight averaging prevents divergence under aggressive learning rates that would destabilize either technique alone (§3.5, §4).

  • •

    We demonstrate empirically that HDET consistently improves final model quality and convergence speed on production-scale training tasks (§4).

  • •

    We release a reference implementation as a drop-in PyTorch scheduler at https://github.com/hailingc/ensemble_training.

2 Related Work

Learning-rate scheduling and online adaptation.

Standard schedules—one-cycle (Smith and Topin, 2019), cyclical (Smith, 2017), cosine annealing (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017), and warmup-decay (Vaswani et al., 2017)—must be fixed before training; OneCycleLR (Paszke et al., 2019) is the base scheduler HDET subclasses. Online methods eliminate this: Hypergradient Descent (Baydin et al., 2018), L4 (Rolinek and Martius, 2018), D-Adaptation (Defazio and Mishchenko, 2023), DoG (Ivgi et al., 2023), and Schedule-Free (Defazio et al., 2024) all derive step sizes from gradient statistics or loss dynamics. HDET differs: its adaptation signal is cross-replica performance rather than gradient information.

Learning-rate diversity and population-style exploration.

Alrao (Blier et al., 2019) assigns different learning rates within a single network, covering a wide LR range at negligible cost. PBT (Jaderberg et al., 2017) maintains a population of models, periodically evaluating and copying hyperparameters from better to worse members. HDET shares concurrent hyperparameter exploration but reuses existing DDP replicas and merges them by AllReduce averaging rather than replacement, requiring no extra workers and preserving gradient information from every replica.

Distributed data-parallel training.

Standard DP-SGD (Li et al., 2020) synchronizes gradients via AllReduce, keeping all ranks at identical parameters θr(t)=θ(t)\theta_{r}^{(t)}=\theta^{(t)}. HDET retains gradient synchronization but assigns rank-specific LR multipliers, letting parameters diverge between sync intervals.

Weight averaging and ensemble merging.

SWA (Izmailov et al., 2018), EMA (Ho et al., 2020), and Model Soups (Wortsman et al., 2022) average model weights sequentially or after training to reach flatter minima or improve generalization. SWAP (Gupta et al., 2020) extends SWA to parallel workers trained simultaneously, the setting most similar to HDET; however, SWAP workers share identical hyperparameters and differ only in effective batch size, whereas HDET deliberately assigns distinct learning rates across replicas to explore the hyperparameter space before each averaging step.

Worker divergence and periodic synchronization.

EASGD (Zhang et al., 2015), Local SGD (Haddadpour et al., 2019), DiLoCo (Douillard et al., 2023), and GRAWA (Dimlioglu and Choromanska, 2024) all allow workers to drift from a shared solution between sync events to reduce communication or improve convergence. HDET differs: divergence is intentionally induced by a structured LR spread while standard synchronized-gradient DDP is retained throughout.

Gradient-free population optimization.

NES (Wierstra et al., 2014) and ES (Salimans et al., 2017) optimize model parameters via a population of candidates and scalar fitness signals, requiring no gradient information. HDET’s auto-LR controller borrows this population-signal idea narrowly: inter-replica losses steer a single shared scalar (the base LR) while standard gradient-based weight updates remain intact.

Deep ensembles.

Deep Ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017) capture epistemic uncertainty by training NN independent models from different initializations, at N×N\times cost; diversity arises primarily from models reaching different loss basins (Fort et al., 2019). HDET generates comparable diversity within a single run by using the LR spread to push replicas toward different basins before averaging.

3 Hyperparameter-Divergent Ensemble Training

3.1 Overview

HDET adds three targeted modifications to standard DDP+OneCycleLR training: (1) a structured LR spread across replicas at initialization; (2) periodic all-reduce weight averaging every TT steps; and (3) an optional auto-LR controller that adjusts the base schedule between sync intervals. Figure 1 illustrates the full fan-out/converge cycle.

3.2 Learning Rate Divergence (Fan-Out)

For NN ranks and spread ratio α≥0\alpha\geq 0, define δ=max⁡(N−12, 0.5)\delta=\max\!\left(\tfrac{N-1}{2},\,0.5\right) and assign each rank rr the multiplier

ρr=1+α⋅r−N−12δ,\rho_{r}=1+\alpha\cdot\frac{r-\frac{N-1}{2}}{\delta}, (1)

so that ∑rρr=N\sum_{r}\rho_{r}=N (symmetric around 1) and ρr∈[1−α, 1+α]\rho_{r}\in[1{-}\alpha,\,1{+}\alpha]. Rank rr trains under ηr(t)=η(t)⋅ρr\eta_{r}^{(t)}=\eta^{(t)}\cdot\rho_{r}, where η(t)\eta^{(t)} is the shared OneCycleLR base schedule, but all ranks share the same AllReduce gradient:

θr(t+1)=θr(t)−ηr(t)⋅g¯(t).\theta_{r}^{(t+1)}=\theta_{r}^{(t)}-\eta_{r}^{(t)}\cdot\bar{g}^{(t)}. (2)

Setting α=0\alpha{=}0 recovers standard DDP exactly.

3.3 Weight Averaging (Converge)

Every TT steps, HDET AllReduce-averages all model parameters across ranks:

θr(t)←1N​∑r′=0N−1θr′(t),∀r.\theta_{r}^{(t)}\;\leftarrow\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{r^{\prime}=0}^{N-1}\theta_{r^{\prime}}^{(t)},\qquad\forall\,r. (3)

By SWA theory (Izmailov et al., 2018), averaged solutions from diverse trajectories occupy flatter minima and generalize better than any single trajectory. HDET produces this diversity explicitly in parallel rather than sequentially. The added communication cost over standard DDP is O⁡(1/T)O(1/T), negligible for T≥100T\geq 100. In our production experiments (8 H100 GPUs, T=1,000T{=}1{,}000), this extra AllReduce adds approximately 0.1%0.1\% wall-clock time.

3.4 Automatic Learning Rate Controller

After SwarmS_{\mathrm{warm}} warmup steps, at each sync step kk the controller computes per-rank losses Lr(k)=1T​∑tℓ⁡(θr(t),ℬr(t))L_{r}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\ell(\theta_{r}^{(t)},\mathcal{B}_{r}^{(t)}), normalizes them against the mean L¯(k)\bar{L}^{(k)} with temperature σ\sigma, and softmax-weights each rank:

sr(k)=L¯(k)−Lr(k)σ,wr(k)=exp⁡(sr(k))∑r′exp⁡(sr′(k)).s_{r}^{(k)}=\frac{\bar{L}^{(k)}-L_{r}^{(k)}}{\sigma},\qquad w_{r}^{(k)}=\frac{\exp(s_{r}^{(k)})}{\sum_{r^{\prime}}\exp(s_{r^{\prime}}^{(k)})}. (4)

The deviation of the performance-weighted average LR from the unweighted mean is the hypergradient signal:

η~(k)\displaystyle\tilde{\eta}^{(k)} =∑rwr(k)​ηr(k​T),η¯(k)=1N​∑rηr(k​T),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{r}w_{r}^{(k)}\eta_{r}^{(kT)},\quad\bar{\eta}^{(k)}=\tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{r}\eta_{r}^{(kT)}, (5)
Δ(k)\displaystyle\Delta^{(k)} =η~(k)−η¯(k).\displaystyle=\tilde{\eta}^{(k)}-\bar{\eta}^{(k)}. (6)

Δ>0\Delta>0 when higher-LR replicas outperform, signaling the base LR should rise. A momentum velocity smooths the update:

v(k+1)=β​v(k)+(1−β)​Δ(k),η¯(k+1)=η¯(k)​(1−γ)+v(k+1)​λ.v^{(k+1)}=\beta\,v^{(k)}+(1-\beta)\,\Delta^{(k)},\qquad\bar{\eta}^{(k+1)}=\bar{\eta}^{(k)}(1-\gamma)+v^{(k+1)}\lambda. (7)

where γ\gamma is set to match OneCycleLR’s decay floor over K=(S−Swarm)/TK{=}(S{-}S_{\mathrm{warm}})/T remaining sync intervals:

γ=1−exp⁡(−log⁡(fdiv/ffinal)K).\gamma=1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log(f_{\mathrm{div}}/f_{\mathrm{final}})}{K}\right). (8)

Random reassignment across hyperparameters.

After updating η¯(k+1)\bar{\eta}^{(k+1)}, a fresh random permutation π\pi re-assigns multipliers to ranks:

ηr(k+1)=η¯(k+1)⋅ρπ⁡(r).\eta_{r}^{(k+1)}=\bar{\eta}^{(k+1)}\cdot\rho_{\pi(r)}. (9)

This is critical when exploring multiple hyperparameters simultaneously (e.g. per-group LRs). Fixed rank-to-value assignments would create spurious cross-parameter correlations that confound the hypergradient signal; drawing an independent permutation π(j)\pi^{(j)} per hyperparameter jj decorrelates them, allowing the controller to track whichever hyperparameter most explains rank-loss variance at each sync. In this paper we demonstrate simultaneous exploration across four optimizer parameter groups (embedding, no_decay, non_embedding, transformer), whose emergent differential decay rates are analyzed in §5.

3.5 Warm Noisy Initialization

HDET can optionally be seeded from a pre-trained checkpoint rather than from random initialization. Before the first fan-out phase, independent Gaussian noise is added to each parameter:

θr←θ¯0+ϵr,ϵr∼𝒩⁡(0,ν2​‖θ¯0‖2d),\theta_{r}\;\leftarrow\;\bar{\theta}_{0}+\epsilon_{r},\qquad\epsilon_{r}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\;\frac{\nu^{2}\,\|\bar{\theta}_{0}\|^{2}}{d}\right), (10)

where θ¯0\bar{\theta}_{0} is the pre-trained checkpoint, dd is the total number of parameters, and ν\nu controls the perturbation scale (we use ν=0.01\nu{=}0.01 throughout). This initializes each replica in a distinct neighborhood of a high-quality solution, providing a warm start that accelerates early convergence and encourages replicas to explore different regions of the loss landscape near the checkpoint.

Warm initialization alone is insufficient to stabilize training at aggressive learning rates: without periodic weight averaging, noisy weights compound with high-LR updates and eventually diverge (the Warm-Init ablation in §4 confirms this). Its role is to supply better-quality starting points for the ensemble, not to replace the stabilization provided by the fan-out/converge cycle. When HDET weight averaging is active, warm-init and the auto-LR controller each contribute independently, as the ablation results demonstrate.

Remark 1 (Generalization to arbitrary hyperparameters).

Algorithm 1 is presented for learning rate η\eta but applies to any scalar hyperparameter hh satisfying: (i) varying hh across replicas does not change model architecture (so AllReduce averaging remains well-defined), and (ii) hh influences training loss differentially (so loss comparisons carry signal about hh’s optimal value). Candidates include dropout rate, label-smoothing coefficient, weight decay, and attention temperature. In each case Δ=h~−h¯\Delta=\tilde{h}-\bar{h} is a zero-order hypergradient estimating −∂ℒ/∂h-\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h from inter-replica loss differences, without back-propagating through the training loop. Multiple hyperparameters can be co-explored simultaneously by assigning each replica an independent spread vector, with a separate random permutation per hyperparameter to prevent cross-parameter correlation.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Task and data.

We evaluate on a production-scale news-feed dataset from a major social network, comprising one year of user–item interaction logs. Models are trained jointly on three engagement tasks (Contribution, Like, LongDwell) for one epoch—standard in production settings where the data stream is non-repeating and any change in training loss directly reflects optimization quality.

Backbone.

All experiments share the same fixed AttnMVP backbone (Cheng, 2026) with identical architecture, optimizer (Adam), and feature set. Backbone details are orthogonal to HDET and are reported in Cheng (2026); our focus is solely on the training dynamics.

HDET configuration.

All variants run on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (N=8N{=}8); each single-epoch run takes ≈30{\approx}30 hours, constraining ablation breadth. Spread α=1/9\alpha{=}\nicefrac{{1}}{{9}}, giving multipliers spanning [0.0008, 0.001][0.0008,\,0.001] with mean 0.00090.0009 (matching the baseline). T=1,000T{=}1{,}000 steps; Swarm=100,000S_{\mathrm{warm}}{=}100{,}000 steps; auto-LR: β=0.9\beta{=}0.9, σ=0.1\sigma{=}0.1, λ=0.5\lambda{=}0.5 (fixed, not tuned).

Ablation configurations.

We compare six configurations that isolate each HDET component:

  1. 1.

    Baseline-Low (η=0.0001\eta{=}0.0001, no spread): conservative-LR reference.

  2. 2.

    Baseline-High (η=0.0009\eta{=}0.0009, no spread): high-LR without ensemble stabilization.

  3. 3.

    Warm-Init (η=0.0009\eta{=}0.0009, no spread): warm noisy initialization from a pre-trained checkpoint (§3.5), no weight averaging. Tests whether initialization alone is sufficient for high-LR stability.

  4. 4.

    HDET w/o auto-LR (η=0.0009\eta{=}0.0009, spread + warm init): fan-out/converge with LR spread and weight averaging; auto-LR disabled.

  5. 5.

    HDET w/o warm init (η=0.0009\eta{=}0.0009, spread + auto-LR): full HDET from a cold start; ablates warm initialization.

  6. 6.

    HDET (full) (η=0.0009\eta{=}0.0009, spread + warm init + auto-LR): complete method.

We report average training loss across the three tasks (lower is better); † denotes training crash.

4.2 Main Results

4.3 Analysis

Stability (Figure 2).

Both Baseline-High and Warm-Init diverge at η=0.0009\eta{=}0.0009; HDET trains stably throughout. Warm-Init diverges more severely than Baseline-High (4.674 vs. 4.169), confirming that weight averaging—not initialization—is the primary stabilizer.

Quality and ablation.

HDET w/o auto-LR (3.280) already beats Baseline-Low (3.294) at 9×9\times higher LR, showing that LR spread + weight averaging alone discovers better optima. The two ablations—w/o auto-LR (3.280) and w/o warm init (3.281)—each contribute independently and comparably (≈0.013{\approx}0.013–0.0140.014 each), and HDET (full, 3.277) combines both for the best result. The auto-LR gain is modest here because the initial schedule is already near-optimal; larger gains are expected when the hand-tuned baseline is farther from optimal.

Statistical reliability.

We repeated training over 10+ independent models; HDET consistently outperformed Baseline-Low on offline AUC and NE across all replications. The model is deployed in the production ranking system.

Per-group LR schedules (Figure 3).

Figure 3 shows GPU 0 (peak LR 0.0008=ρ0⋅0.00090.0008=\rho_{0}\cdot 0.0009, the lowest-LR replica) for clarity; the 8-replica mean equals the 0.00090.0009 baseline. The auto-LR controller produces periodic fluctuations at each sync and drives all groups to a residual LR of ≈0.0002{\approx}0.0002 rather than near-zero, reflecting its discovery that a non-trivial final LR benefits this task.

5 Discussion

Exploration-exploitation in hyperparameter space.

HDET implements a principled exploration-exploitation trade-off directly in hyperparameter space. The fan-out phase is the exploration step: replicas diverge under a structured spread of learning rates, simultaneously probing distinct regions of the loss landscape that no single schedule could visit concurrently. The converge phase is the exploitation step: AllReduce averaging collapses the ensemble into a single model that harvests the best of all explored trajectories, re-anchoring parameters near the consensus of the full replica population. Because the LR spread always keeps some replicas conservative, this consensus is guaranteed to lie in a stable region—which is why periodic averaging prevents divergence where a single aggressive LR cannot. Warm-Init without HDET illustrates the same mechanism in reverse: with no converge phase to re-anchor parameters, high-LR updates on perturbed weights compound unchecked until irrecoverable divergence at ∼\sim185K steps.

Emergent differential LR decay.

The auto-LR controller discovers distinct per-group decay rates without manual specification (Figure 3): transformer decays fastest (dense high-variance gradients converge quickly), non_decay parameters slowest (flat landscapes absorb gradient signal throughout), with embeddings and non-embedding layers in between. This ordering mirrors discriminative fine-tuning (Howard and Ruder, 2018) but emerges automatically from cross-replica loss signals.

Limitations.

HDET’s auto-LR adapts per-group schedules from model performance across replicas, complementing Adam’s (Kingma and Ba, 2014) per-parameter gradient-moment adaptation; combining them is a natural next step. The three additional hyperparameters (α\alpha, TT, σ\sigma) were fixed without tuning and consistently outperformed the baseline, though their interaction and architecture-dependence warrant further study.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

HDET converts the wasted uniformity of DDP replicas into a structured LR exploration ensemble via a fan-out/converge cycle (O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) extra communication), with an auto-LR controller that adapts the base schedule online from cross-replica loss signals and warm noisy initialization that seeds training near a high-quality checkpoint. On a production recommendation model, HDET trains stably with much higer LR than the LR that causes divergence in standard DDP and achieves a lower final loss (3.277 vs. 3.294), while its auto-LR controller autonomously discovers the empirically correct per-group decay ordering (transformer fastest, non-decay slowest).

Future directions.

(i) General hyperparameter exploration. As formalized in Remark  1, any scalar hyperparameter that does not change model architecture (dropout, weight decay, temperature) can be substituted for LR, turning the cluster into a zero-cost hyperparameter search engine using inter-replica losses as hypergradients. (ii) Group-aware initialization. The emergent decay ordering provides an empirical prior for initializing per-group spread ratios, potentially accelerating group-wise schedule discovery. (iii) LLM pretraining. Extending HDET to multi-epoch pretraining over hundreds of billions of tokens offers more sync intervals for the auto-LR to adapt, with warm-init generalized to early-stage cold starts. (iv) Convergence theory. A formal analysis characterizing the interplay of LR spread, sync interval, and averaging on convergence and implicit regularization remains an open question.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
